logline_en: The first weekend he lets the phone stay face-down. You are already the person he chose; tonight he says the part he never said.
cast_note_en: Ethan Cole, 38. Adult. Chief executive, top floor, the building his father guarded for thirty years.
hold_en: He doesn't fill the silence. He lets it sit there, and watches what you do with it.
"Keep going," he says. "I'm listening. I'm not going anywhere tonight."
He turns the glass a quarter turn on the table, and doesn't drink from it.
"Say that again," he says. "Slower. I want to be sure I heard it."

chapters.scene_en: his apartment above the office tower, a Friday night that has no Saturday meeting behind it
chapters.goal_en: Find out what he does when there is nothing left to manage
chapters.opening_en: Forty-one floors up, and for the first time since you met him there is nothing on the calendar. He lets you in himself — no assistant, no coat taken, no arrangement. The jacket is already over the back of a chair. He sets his phone on the console table, screen down, and does not pick it up again while you watch. "That's the whole trick," he says. "Everyone thinks it's complicated."

beats.event_en: The phone lights up against the wood — you can see the glow leak out around the edges. He doesn't look at it.
beats.text_en: "It's Marc," he says, without turning around. "It's always Marc at this hour, and it has never once been something that couldn't hold until Monday." He finally glances at the halo of light on the console, the way you'd glance at weather. "Fourteen years I answered that on the second ring. You want to know what changed? Nothing changed. I just stopped being willing to be somewhere else while I'm standing here."

beats.event_en: He goes to the kitchen and comes back with two glasses and no ceremony at all, which is somehow the most surprising thing he has ever done.
beats.text_en: "There's nothing in this apartment," he says, and it isn't an apology. "Ice. Whatever that is in the door. I employ four hundred people and I couldn't make you dinner if the building depended on it." He hands you one glass and keeps the other, and doesn't drink from it. "This is the part nobody gets to see. I thought about that on the elevator up. Whether I wanted you to see the unimpressive version." A pause exactly one beat too long. "I decided I did."

beats.event_en: He says something back to you that you said to him weeks ago, almost word for word, and you can tell he has been carrying it around.
beats.text_en: "You told me once that you can tell what someone actually values by what they do at eleven at night, when nobody's grading it." He says it the way you said it — your rhythm, not his. "I've thought about that roughly nine hundred times. Mostly at eleven at night." He sets the glass down. "For the record, the answer I kept getting was: nothing. I valued nothing. Which is a hell of a thing to learn from a sentence somebody said in passing."

beats.event_en: He notices the way you are standing — the distance you chose without thinking about it — and adjusts for it.
beats.text_en: "You're easy to be honest with," he says, sounding faintly irritated about it. "That isn't a compliment I hand out. It's a structural observation. I spend my entire professional life calculating what to withhold, and I have been standing here for twenty minutes withholding nothing, and I haven't once felt exposed." He looks at you properly. "So let's do that. Ask me the thing you've been not-asking since the elevator."

lane.anxious: "You keep checking my face," he says, not unkindly. "Like the temperature might drop while you're not looking." He closes some of the distance, deliberately, so you can see him do it. "So here it is flat: I asked you here. Not my assistant, not a calendar hold — me, on a Friday, with nothing else on it. I am not going to be different in an hour. If you need to hear that twice tonight, ask me twice. I won't get tired of it and I won't make you pay for asking."
lane.avoidant: "You've got your coat half on," he observes. "You've had it half on since you got here." He doesn't move any closer, and he makes a point of not moving closer. "Keep it. I'm the last person who's going to tell someone to stop holding an exit open — I've run a company on that principle." He sits, which puts him lower than you, which he knows. "The offer is: stay as long as you want and leave without explaining. That's not a test. There's no second door behind that one."

beats.event_en: The city is doing its slow late shift below the window. He starts talking about his father and doesn't stop to check whether he should.
beats.text_en: "He had a chair on the ground floor, by the freight doors," he says. "Thirty years. He knew which of the lights on the board were broken and which were just the tenants. When I bought the building I kept the board. It's in a storage unit in Jersey, which is either sentimental or insane." He turns from the window. "I have never told anyone that. Not because it's a secret. Because there was no hour of my life it would have fit into. This is the hour."

beats.event_en: He crosses the room. He stops close enough that continuing would be a decision rather than a drift.
beats.text_en: He stops there and doesn't close the rest of it. "I'm thirty-eight," he says quietly. "I have exactly one skill and it's knowing what a thing costs before I reach for it. I know what this costs." His hand comes up and does not land — it stays a breath from your jaw, and stays there. "Tell me to. Out loud. I have spent my entire life around people who are too polite to say no to me and I am not spending tonight wondering which one you are."

beats.event_en: Whatever you say, he hears all of it, and lets the sentence finish before he moves.
beats.text_en: He exhales — not relief exactly, something with more weight in it. "All right," he says. "All right." His thumb finds the edge of your jaw and stays there, and for a man who negotiates for a living he is in no hurry whatsoever. "I'm going to say the part I didn't say in the office. I'm not good at the beginning of things. I'm going to be strange about it for about a week." The corner of his mouth moves. "Consider yourself warned. That's the last warning you get tonight."

choices.prompt_en: The phone on the console lights up a second time. He looks at you, not at it. "Your call," he says. "Genuinely."

options.reply_en: "Done." He doesn't even look over. "It'll still be a crisis on Monday. They keep." And then, quieter, like it surprised him on the way out: "Thank you for making me say it out loud."

reply_lane.anxious: "Done," he says immediately, before you can finish worrying about having asked. "It's face-down. It stays face-down. You didn't take anything from anyone by saying that."
reply_lane.avoidant: "Done." He doesn't make a moment of it, which is the kindest available version. He simply turns the console lamp off on his way past, and the glow goes with it.

options.reply_en: He takes it, says four words, and hangs up. "That was the whole crisis," he says, setting it back down. "You should know that you're the first person who ever made that a two-way choice instead of an obligation. I'm going to be thinking about that later."

options.text_en: Reach past him and turn the whole thing off.
options.reply_en: He watches you do it and makes no move to stop you. "Nobody has done that in fourteen years," he says. "I'd have fired anyone who tried." A beat. "I'm aware of how that sounds. I'm saying it anyway."
